title: Sequence
body: A sequence is a function from the whole numbers to the real numbers, so its graph is a set of discrete points rather than a curve.
ced_evidence: 2.1.A.1 "A sequence is a function from the whole numbers to the real numbers."

title: Arithmetic sequence general term
body: a_n = a_0 + dn \quad\text{or}\quad a_n = a_k + d(n-k)
ced_evidence: 2.1.A.3 "an = a0 + dn ... or by an = ak + d(n - k)"

title: Geometric sequence general term
body: g_n = g_0 r^{n} \quad\text{or}\quad g_n = g_k r^{\,n-k}
ced_evidence: 2.1.B.2 "g n = g 0 r^n ... or by g n = g k r^(n-k)"

title: Arithmetic vs. geometric: constant difference vs. constant ratio
body: Arithmetic sequences have a common difference (constant rate of change), while geometric sequences have a common ratio (constant proportional change); an increasing geometric sequence of positive values increases by a larger amount each step.

title: Linear function forms
body: f(x) = b + mx \quad\text{or}\quad f(x) = y_i + m(x - x_i)
ced_evidence: 2.2.A.1, 2.2.A.2 "f(x) = yi + m(x - xi) based on a known slope, m, and a point"

title: Exponential function from a known ratio and a point
ced_evidence: 2.2.A.4 "f(x) = yi b^(x - xi) based on a known ratio, b, and a point, (xi, yi)"

title: Linear vs. exponential: how outputs change over equal-length intervals
body: Over equal-length input intervals, outputs that change at a constant rate (addition) indicate a linear function, and outputs that change proportionally (multiplication) indicate an exponential function whose ratio cannot be 0 or 1.
ced_evidence: 2.2.B.1 "if the output values of a function change proportionally, then the function is exponential. For an exponential function, the known ratio cannot be 0 or 1."

title: Two distinct values determine these sequences and functions
body: Arithmetic sequences, linear functions, geometric sequences, and exponential functions can each be determined by two distinct sequence or function values.
ced_evidence: 2.2.B.3 "can be determined by two distinct sequence or function values"

title: General form of an exponential function
body: f(x) = ab^{x},\quad a \neq 0,\; b > 0,\; b \neq 1
ced_evidence: 2.3.A.1 "f(x) = ab^x, with the initial value a, where a ≠ 0, and the base b, where b > 0, and b ≠ 1"

title: Exponential growth and exponential decay
body: For f(x)=ab^x, exponential growth occurs when a>0 and b>1, and exponential decay occurs when a>0 and 0<b<1.
ced_evidence: 2.3.A.1 "When a > 0 and b > 1 ... exponential growth ... 0 < b < 1 ... exponential decay"

title: Shape and extrema of exponential functions
body: The domain of an exponential function is all real numbers; it is always increasing or always decreasing, always concave up or always concave down, with no extrema except on a closed interval and no points of inflection.
ced_evidence: 2.3.A.2, 2.3.A.3 "always increasing or always decreasing ... do not have extrema except on a closed interval"

title: End behavior of exponential functions
body: \lim_{x\to\pm\infty} ab^{x} = \infty,\quad \lim_{x\to\pm\infty} ab^{x} = -\infty,\quad\text{or}\quad \lim_{x\to\pm\infty} ab^{x} = 0
caution: For a given function, the limit as x→+∞ and as x→−∞ are different cases; one end is unbounded and the other approaches 0.
ced_evidence: 2.3.A.5 "the output values will increase or decrease without bound or will get arbitrarily close to zero"

title: Additive transformation of an exponential function
body: If outputs of f are not proportional over equal-length input intervals but outputs of an additive transformation of f are, then f can be modeled by an additive transformation of an exponential function.
ced_evidence: 2.3.A.4; 2.5.A.2 "A constant may need to be added to the dependent variable values"

title: Product property for exponents and horizontal translation
body: b^{m}b^{n} = b^{m+n};\quad b^{x+k} = b^{k}b^{x} = ab^{x},\ a = b^{k}
ced_evidence: 2.4.A.1 "every horizontal translation of an exponential function ... is equivalent to a vertical dilation"

title: Power property for exponents and horizontal dilation
body: (b^{m})^{n} = b^{mn};\quad b^{cx} = (b^{c})^{x},\ c \neq 0
ced_evidence: 2.4.A.2 "every horizontal dilation of an exponential function ... is equivalent to a change of the base"

title: Negative exponent and unit-fraction exponent
body: b^{-n} = \frac{1}{b^{n}};\quad b^{1/k} = \sqrt[k]{b}\ \text{(when it exists)}
ced_evidence: 2.4.A.3, 2.4.A.4 "the kth root of b, when it exists"

title: Building an exponential model from two input-output pairs
body: An exponential model can be built from a ratio and initial value, or from two input-output pairs by solving the resulting system of equations for the initial value a and base b; with technology, use an exponential regression.
ced_evidence: 2.5.A.3, 2.5.A.5 "solving a system of equations resulting from the two input-output pairs"

title: Natural base e
body: The natural base e, approximately 2.718, is often used as the base of exponential functions that model contextual scenarios.
ced_evidence: 2.5.A.6 "The natural base e, which is approximately 2.718"

title: Base as growth factor and percent change
body: In f(x)=ab^x the base b is the growth factor for each unit change in input and relates to a percent change in context.
ced_evidence: 2.5.B.1 "the base of the exponent, b, can be understood as a growth factor in successive unit changes"

title: Equivalent exponential forms reveal different rates
caution: The first form shows a factor of 2 per day; the second shows a factor of 2^7 per week. State the time unit for the factor in context.
ced_evidence: 2.5.B.2 "increases by a factor of 2 every day ... by a factor of 2^7 every week"

title: Model use limited by context domain
body: Models predict dependent-variable values within contextual domain constraints and can also be used to determine independent-variable values.
ced_evidence: 2.5.B.3 "depending on the contextual constraints on the domain"

title: Residual
body: \text{residual} = y_{\text{actual}} - y_{\text{predicted}}
ced_evidence: 2.6.B.1 "the actual value of the dependent variable value minus the value predicted by the function regression model"

title: Residual plot
body: A graph of residuals against the independent variable; the model is justified as appropriate if the plot appears without pattern.

items.label: No pattern
items.meaning: Model justified as appropriate for the data set

caution: Justify the model by stating that the residual plot shows no pattern.
ced_evidence: 2.6.B.1 "A model is justified as appropriate for a data set if the residual plot appears without pattern."

title: Model errors: over- and underestimates
body: Errors can be viewed as signed differences or unsigned absolute values of residuals, and may show the model underestimates or overestimates actual values on an input interval; the context may indicate which is preferred.
ced_evidence: 2.6.B.2 "Errors may reveal that the model underestimates or overestimates actual values"

title: Choosing among linear, quadratic, and exponential models
body: Data with a slightly changing rate of change can be modeled by linear, quadratic, or exponential functions, and the most appropriate model is chosen using contextual clues and applicability.

title: Composite function
body: (f\circ g)(x) = f(g(x))
caution: The domain is restricted to input values of g whose outputs lie in the domain of f.
ced_evidence: 2.7.A.1 "the domain of the composite function is restricted to those input values of g for which the corresponding output value is in the domain of f"

title: Composition is not commutative
body: f∘g and g∘f are typically different functions, so f(g(x)) and g(f(x)) are typically different values.
ced_evidence: 2.7.A.3 "The composition of functions is not commutative"

title: Identity function
body: f(x)=x;\quad g(f(x)) = f(g(x)) = g(x)
ced_evidence: 2.7.A.4 "The function f(x) = x is called the identity function."

title: Building and decomposing compositions
body: To build f(g(x)) analytically, substitute g(x) for every x in f; to decompose, write the function as simpler functions where the variable of one replaces each instance of the inner function; translations are composition with x+k and dilations are composition with kx.
ced_evidence: 2.7.B.2, 2.7.C.1, 2.7.C.2 "composition of g(x) = x + k with f", 2.7.C.3 "g(x) = kx"

title: Invertible function and inverse function
body: A function is invertible on a specified domain if each output is mapped from a unique input; its inverse maps outputs back to inputs so that f(a)=b means f^{-1}(b)=a.

title: Composition of a function and its inverse
ced_evidence: 2.8.B.1 "The composition of a function, f, and its inverse function, f^-1, is the identity function"

title: Ways to find an inverse
body: Representations of the inverse of y=f(x) on an invertible domain.

items.label: Table
items.meaning: Reverse input-output pairs: (a, b) becomes (b, a); domain and range swap

items.label: Graph
items.meaning: Reflect the graph over the identity function h(x)=x

items.label: Equation
items.meaning: Reverse the roles of x and y in y=f(x), then solve for y=f^{-1}(x)

title: Contextual restrictions on inverses
body: Beyond restricting the domain to obtain an inverse, contextual restrictions may limit where an inverse function applies.
ced_evidence: 2.8.B.5 "contextual restrictions may also limit the applicability of an inverse function"

title: Definition of a logarithm
body: \log_b c = a \iff b^{a} = c,\quad b>0,\ b\neq 1
caution: With no base written, log means the common logarithm with base 10.
ced_evidence: 2.9.A.1 "log b c = a if and only if b^a = c"

title: Logarithmic scale
body: On a logarithmic scale each unit represents a multiplicative change of the base of the logarithm, e.g. base 10 units are 10^0, 10^1, 10^2, ….
ced_evidence: 2.9.A.3 "each unit represents a multiplicative change of the base of the logarithm"

title: General form of a logarithmic function
body: f(x) = a\log_b x,\quad b>0,\ b\neq 1,\ a\neq 0
ced_evidence: 2.10.A.1 "f(x) = a log b x, with base b, where b > 0, b ≠ 1, and a ≠ 0"

title: Logarithmic and exponential functions are inverses
body: f(x)=\log_b x,\ g(x)=b^{x}:\quad g(f(x)) = f(g(x)) = x
ced_evidence: 2.10.A.3 "f(x) = log b x and g(x) = b^x ... are inverse functions"

title: Graph and ordered pairs of log vs. exponential
body: The graph of log_b x is the reflection of b^x over y=x, and if (s,t) is on g(x)=b^x then (t,s) is on f(x)=log_b x.
ced_evidence: 2.10.A.4, 2.10.A.5 "then (t, s) is an ordered pair of the logarithmic function"

title: Exponential growth vs. logarithmic growth
body: Exponential growth has outputs changing multiplicatively as inputs change additively; logarithmic growth has outputs changing additively as inputs change multiplicatively.
ced_evidence: 2.10.A.2 "exponential growth is characterized by output values changing multiplicatively as input values change additively"

title: Domain, range, and shape of logarithmic functions
body: A general-form logarithmic function has domain x>0 and range all real numbers; it is always increasing or always decreasing, always concave up or always concave down, with no extrema except on a closed interval and no points of inflection.

title: End behavior and asymptote of logarithmic functions
body: \lim_{x\to 0^{+}} a\log_b x = \pm\infty,\quad \lim_{x\to\infty} a\log_b x = \pm\infty;\ \text{vertical asymptote } x=0
ced_evidence: 2.11.A.4 "vertically asymptotic to x = 0, with an end behavior that is unbounded"

title: Recognizing logarithmic behavior via additive transformation
body: For g(x)=f(x+k) with k≠0 and f logarithmic, inputs are not proportional over equal-length output intervals; if inputs of g(x)=f(x+k) are proportional over equal-length output intervals for some function f, then f is logarithmic.

title: Product property for logarithms and horizontal dilation
body: \log_b(xy) = \log_b x + \log_b y;\quad \log_b(kx) = \log_b k + \log_b x
ced_evidence: 2.12.A.1 "every horizontal dilation of a logarithmic function ... is equivalent to a vertical translation"

title: Power property for logarithms
body: \log_b x^{n} = n\log_b x
ced_evidence: 2.12.A.2 "log b x^n = n log b x"

title: Change of base property
body: \log_b x = \frac{\log_a x}{\log_a b},\quad a>0,\ a\neq 1
ced_evidence: 2.12.A.3 "This implies that all logarithmic functions are vertical dilations of each other."

title: Natural logarithm
body: \ln x = \log_e x
ced_evidence: 2.12.A.4 "ln x = log e x"

title: Rewriting an exponential in a different base
body: b^{x} = c^{(\log_c b)(x)}
ced_evidence: 2.13.A.3 "Specifically, b^x = c^((log_c b)(x))"

title: Check for extraneous solutions
body: After solving exponential or logarithmic equations, examine results for extraneous solutions ruled out by mathematical or contextual limitations (e.g. b^x is always positive and log arguments must be positive).
caution: State explicitly which candidate solutions are rejected and why.
ced_evidence: 2.13.A.2 "results should be examined for extraneous solutions precluded by the mathematical or contextual limitations"

title: Transformed exponential and logarithmic forms to invert
body: f(x) = ab^{x+h} + k;\quad f(x) = a\log_b(x+h) + k
ced_evidence: 2.13.B.1, 2.13.B.2 "combination of additive transformations"; "determining the inverse operations to reverse the mapping"

title: Constructing logarithmic models
body: A logarithmic model is built from a proportion and a real zero or from two input-output pairs, by transformations of f(x)=a log_b x, or with a logarithmic regression, and can predict dependent values or determine independent values.
ced_evidence: 2.14.A.2 "an appropriate proportion and a real zero or from two input-output pairs"; 2.14.A.3; 2.14.A.4; 2.14.A.6

title: Semi-log plot
body: A plot in which one axis is logarithmically scaled with base n > 1; when the y-axis is log-scaled, exponential data or functions appear linear.
ced_evidence: 2.15.A.1 "logarithmically scaled with logarithm base n, where n > 1 ... will appear linear"

title: Semi-log linearization of an exponential model
body: y = ab^{x}\ \longrightarrow\ \log_n y = (\log_n b)\,x + \log_n a
caution: Slope of the semi-log line is log_n b and the initial linear value is log_n a, not b and a.
ced_evidence: 2.15.B.2 "y = (log n b) x + log n a ... the linear rate of change is log n b, and the initial linear value is log n a"

title: Using a semi-log plot to justify an exponential model
body: If the logarithms of output values trend linear for large inputs, transformations of an exponential function can model the data, and the dependent values need not be shifted by a constant to see this.
ced_evidence: 2.15.A.2 "the dependent variable values do not need to be transformed by a constant"
